perspective:
I am Ethan. I know Gary and I have been close friends since middle school. Gary is a doctor. I noticed he was working excessively long hours at the hospital, often skipping meals and sacrificing sleep. I invited him to a weekend retreat for relaxation and rejuvenation, telling him his health matters and that two days might give him a new perspective. Gary declined, saying he couldn’t because there was too much to do at the hospital.

At the retreat, I observed Gary acting restless and avoiding discussions about work. I suspected his overworking was about more than professional obligations. I confronted him, saying that since middle school he can tell me anything and that I’m there to help, not judge. He said it was complicated and that he didn’t want to burden me. He then opened up about the pressures of managing a new department and personal challenges. I felt relief and empathy, and I offered to help him find better balance by prioritizing tasks and delegating responsibilities. Gary agreed, saying he could use help organizing his schedule to make time for himself too.

Over the following months, I regularly checked in with Gary, and we discussed his progress and remaining challenges. I saw him making efforts to change, felt hopeful and proud, and continued offering support and encouragement. He told me things were better, that my help meant he wasn’t as overwhelmed, and that he had time for a movie last weekend. After a year, I saw he had adjusted to a healthier work-life balance and could manage on his own. I felt satisfied and happy for him. I decided to step back but told him I’m always just a call away and that he’s got this. He thanked me, said he couldn’t have done it without my support, and felt more in control now.
